 Taylor school district unveils redesign after $130 million bond vote
 The plan calls for a new library, science and arts wings, courtyard spaces, and added security features at Taylor High School
 Noelle Friel , Reporter
 Darrius Smith , Photojournalist
 Published:  October 29, 2026 at 11:36 PM Tags:  Taylor , Wayne County What to know: 
 Taylor High School could get a major renovation. Families and taxpayers got their first look at plans to modernize the school during a community town hall. 
 The project stems from a $130 million bond approved in 2021. Voters originally approved funding for a new high school and career center. 
 The new-school plan was scrapped. District leaders determined during the 2022 design phase that the available funding would not be enough to complete construction. After surveying voters, the district decided to renovate the existing building instead. 
 Renovation plans include major upgrades. Proposed improvements include: A new library. 
 New science and arts wings. 
 Upgraded classrooms. 
 East, north, and central courtyards. 
 Dedicated space for ninth graders. 
 Lockable classroom storage and movable desks. 
 TAYLOR, Mich. — Families and taxpayers got their first look at plans to renovate and modernize Taylor High School during a town hall, five years after voters approved a $130 million bond for a new high school and career center.
 The district scrapped the new-school plan after the 2021 vote when district leaders discovered during the 2022 design phase that they still wouldn’t have the funds to complete construction. After surveying voters, officials opted to renovate the existing high school instead.
 The redesign includes a new library, science and arts wings, upgraded classrooms, and east, north, and central courtyards. 
 Plans also call for dedicated space for ninth graders and classroom improvements, including lockable casework and movable desks for teachers.
 Security features would separate wings, with lockdown doors to isolate parts of the building and security offices spread throughout to help staff respond, according to the district’s presentation.
 Superintendent Mike Wegher said safety was a top priority in the design.
 He pointed to two fights at the high school this week as underscoring the need for security improvements.
 “The biggest thing to me is that hallway layout,” Wegher said. “You heard a lot of it today that the way it currently is can lead to unsafe situations. And to have a simplified floor plan where people can see all the way through is going to help us maintain better safety.”
 The district is partnering with two companies, The Collaborative as architects, and Barton-Malow Builders as construction manager.
 Many attendees said they were glad to see how the bond money would be used, while teachers and other community members said they looked forward to seeing the plans move forward.
 The project will be built in eight phases. 
 The city expects to award bids between February and April 2027, with the first phase scheduled to begin in June. The final phases are expected to wrap up in December 2030.
 The bond proposal called for three bond sales totaling $130 million. So far, only one bond sale, $31 million, took place in April 2022. 
 The school board is scheduled to vote on the design plans and the next set of bond sales at a meeting on Nov. 4. 
 The district broke ground in March on a new sports complex at the school.
